title: Buying at $10, $5, $10
hook: You invest $100 each month while the price dips and recovers. What did a share cost you?

doesNotKnow: that buying equal dollars gets more units when the price is low
that average cost per share differs from the average of the prices

misconception: My average cost per share is the average of the prices.
objective: The learner can explain that equal dollars buy more shares at a low price, so with prices $10, $5, $10 the average cost is $7.50, below the plain average price of $8.33.

claims.text: Putting $100 in at $10, $5 and $10 a share buys 10, 20 and 10 shares: 40 shares for $300.
The average cost per share is $300 / 40 = $7.50.
The plain average of the three prices is $8.33.
The average cost of equal-dollar purchases is the harmonic mean of the prices, which is never above their plain average.
claims.source: Cost per share = n x D / sum(D / p_i) = n / sum(1 / p_i), the harmonic mean; harmonic mean <= arithmetic mean (a standard inequality). Checked on the stage at middle prices $2, $5, $10, $20.

claims.text: Equal dollars buy more shares when the price is low, so the low-price month counts for more.
claims.source: Shares = dollars / price; at $5 the same $100 buys twice as many shares as at $10.

claims.text: The lesson is a model: three equal buys at invented prices; arithmetic only, with no claim about returns or what to buy.
claims.source: Assumptions of Demo.tsx; stage chip 'Model: $100 a month at invented prices'.

recall.question: You spend $60 on a share at $6, then $60 at $3. What is your average cost per share?
recall.why: 60 / 6 = 10 shares and 60 / 3 = 20 shares: 30 shares for $120, or $4 a share, below the plain average price of $4.50.
